controversies/icons-controversy/question: May Christians make and venerate images of Christ, Mary and the saints, or does the second commandment forbid them?
controversies/icons-controversy/summary: The Byzantine iconoclast crisis (726–843) and the Reformation image debates (1520s–1560s) asked the same question with different answers. Nicaea II (787) approved veneration distinct from worship; the Reformed churches removed images from worship; Lutherans treated them as permissible.
controversies/icons-controversy/sides/0/: Of old, God without body or form could never be depicted. But now that God has been seen in the flesh and lived among us, we depict what we have seen. We do not worship matter; we worship the Creator of matter, who became matter for our sake. The honour we give an icon passes to the one it represents — as a kiss given to a letter from a loved one honours the sender.
The incarnation makes God visible and depictable.
The second commandment forbids images in worship.
Popular practice blurs veneration and worship.
controversies/icons-controversy/sides/1/: God has spoken: no graven image. Our armies are defeated and God is angry because his people bow before painted wood. And what does a painter depict when he paints Christ? Either his humanity alone, dividing him like Nestorius, or his Godhead too, circumscribing the infinite. Christ gave us one true image of himself — the holy Eucharist. Honour the saints by imitating their lives.
Christological dilemma: images either divide or confuse Christ's natures.
The Eucharist is the only true image.
An icon depicts the person, not the nature.
Iconoclasm implicitly denies the reality of the incarnation.
controversies/icons-controversy/sides/2/: God will not be represented by the works of our hands; he has given us his Word and his sacraments. The second commandment is not a ceremonial law but a moral one. Churches filled with images teach people to look to wood and stone rather than to hear Christ preached. Let them be removed in good order, and let the people be taught by living preaching, not dumb images.
The second commandment is permanent moral law.
God teaches through the Word, not images (Heidelberg Catechism Q. 98).
Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent when it became an idol.
Lutherans: images are adiaphora; forced removal is legalism.
It undervalues the incarnation and the goodness of matter.
controversies/icons-controversy/timeline: Leo III moves against icons (traditional date).
Patriarch Germanus resigns; John of Damascus writes in defence of images.
Second Council of Nicaea restores icon veneration.
Council of Frankfurt (Charlemagne) and the Libri Carolini criticise Nicaea II, partly through mistranslation.
Empress Theodora restores icons: the Triumph of Orthodoxy.
Karlstadt's On the Removal of Images; Luther's Invocavit sermons urge restraint.
Trent's decree on images; Heidelberg Catechism Q. 96–98.
Beeldenstorm: iconoclastic riots in the Netherlands.
controversies/icons-controversy/resoluti: Resolved for Orthodox and Catholics by Nicaea II (787) and the Triumph of Orthodoxy (843); reopened by the Reformation, which produced a lasting divide: Reformed churches without images in worship, Lutherans and Anglicans with images but without veneration, Catholics and Orthodox with veneration.
controversies/icons-controversy/conseque: Icons became central to Orthodox identity; their theology shaped Christian art East and West.
Loss of much early Byzantine art; destruction of medieval art in Reformed regions.
Different church architecture and worship across confessions.
controversies/marian-dogmas-controversy/: Were the Catholic dogmas of the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption (1950) legitimate developments of apostolic faith, or innovations without warrant?
Immaculate Conception and Assumption: development or innovation?

Pius IX and Pius XII defined two Marian dogmas after worldwide consultation of bishops. Catholics see them as the unfolding of the faith about Mary as Theotokos and new Eve; the Orthodox share belief in Mary's holiness and glorification but reject the Immaculate Conception and the papal mode of definition; Protestants find no scriptural basis.
Catholic

The angel greeted Mary as one already filled with grace. If Christ is the perfect Redeemer, he could redeem his mother in the most perfect way — by preserving her from sin rather than rescuing her from it. The whole Church, East and West, has long sung her as all-holy and celebrated her passing into glory. In 1854 and 1950 the successor of Peter, after consulting the bishops of the world, simply declared what the Church already believed.
Preservative redemption (Scotus).
Luke 1:28 and the new Eve typology.
Ancient liturgical feasts of the Conception and Dormition.
Consultation of the worldwide episcopate showed consensus.
No early or scriptural evidence.
Major medieval doctors opposed the Immaculate Conception.
Genesis 3:15
Luke 1:28
Luke 1:42
Revelation 12:1
Orthodox

We call the Theotokos all-holy, more honourable than the cherubim, and we celebrate her Dormition and translation to heaven every August. But we do not need the Latin dogma of the Immaculate Conception, which depends on a view of inherited guilt we do not hold, and which would set Mary apart from the humanity her Son came to heal. Nor can one bishop make new dogmas binding on the Church.
Mary's holiness is grace and freedom within our fallen condition.
Ancestral sin is inherited mortality, not guilt.
Dogma is defined conciliarly, not by a pope alone.
Orthodox liturgy itself calls Mary spotless and immaculate (achrantos).
Belief in the Dormition-Assumption is essentially shared.
Luke 1:47
Romans 5:12
Psalm 45:9–15
Protestant

We honour Mary as Scripture does: blessed among women, the Lord's handmaid, a model of faith who herself rejoiced in ‘God my Saviour’. But no doctrine can be required for salvation that Scripture does not teach. Neither the Immaculate Conception nor the Assumption appears in the Bible or in the earliest church, and making them dogmas binds consciences where God has not spoken.
No scriptural basis; ‘all have sinned’ (Romans 3:23).
Mary calls God her Saviour (Luke 1:47).
The dogmas exemplify unchecked tradition and papal authority.
Not all truth is explicit in Scripture (Catholic reply).
Luther himself held Mary's holiness in high esteem.

Luke 1:47

Bernard of Clairvaux opposes the new feast of the Conception at Lyon.
Duns Scotus argues for preservative redemption.
Sixtus IV approves the feast of the Conception.
Ineffabilis Deus defines the Immaculate Conception.
Lourdes apparitions to Bernadette Soubirous.
Vatican I defines papal infallibility.
Munificentissimus Deus defines the Assumption.
Lumen Gentium chapter 8 on Mary.
ARCIC's ‘Mary: Grace and Hope in Christ’.

Catholic dogma since 1854 and 1950; rejected as binding by Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches. Ecumenical dialogues (ARCIC 2005; Lutheran–Catholic 1990) record partial convergence on content and continued disagreement on authority.
Strengthened Marian devotion in Catholicism (Lourdes, Fatima, Marian Year).
Added to Orthodox and Protestant objections to papal authority.
Prompted renewed Protestant reflection on Mary's place in Scripture.
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/quest: May Chinese Christians honour their ancestors and Confucius, and call God "Tian" or "Shangdi"?
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/summa: For more than a century Jesuits, Dominicans, Franciscans, popes and Chinese emperors argued whether Confucian and ancestral rites were civil honours compatible with the faith or idolatrous worship, and whether Chinese terms could name God. Rome’s ban (1704–1742) crippled the mission; its reversal (1939) prefigured modern inculturation.
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/sides: The Chinese classics already knew the Lord on High, and honouring ancestors and Confucius is filial piety and civic respect, not worship of gods. Paul quoted the poets of Athens; we must speak to China in its own noble language. To forbid these rites is to tell the Chinese that becoming Christian means ceasing to be Chinese, and to close the empire to the gospel.
Rites include offerings and prayers to spirits

Whatever the scholars say, ordinary Chinese offer food, incense and prayers to the spirits of the dead and to Confucius, expecting blessings. To tolerate such rites is to tolerate idolatry, and to call God by names that the Chinese use for heaven or a deity confuses the Creator with creation. The purity of the faith cannot be traded for imperial favour.
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/timel: Propaganda Fide, on Dominican complaints, first condemns the rites; a 1656 decree permits them on Jesuit representation.
Clement XI condemns the rites; papal legate Tournon’s mission fails.
Kangxi, reading the papal bull Ex illa die (1715), bans Christian preaching.
Ex quo singulari makes the ban final.
Pius XII’s Plane compertum est permits Chinese Catholics to honour Confucius and ancestors.
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/resol: Rome forbade the rites in 1704–1742 and permitted them in 1939, judging that their meaning had become civil; Vatican II’s respect for cultures vindicated much of the accommodation approach. Protestant churches in China, Korea and Japan still debate ancestral rites, often forbidding bowing at ancestral tablets.
controversies/chinese-rites-debate/conse: Imperial restrictions on Christianity in China (1721–1840s).
Contributed to the suppression of the Jesuits (1773).
A paradigm case for later theories of inculturation.
controversies/salvation-of-the-unevangel: Can people who never hear of Christ, or who follow other religions, be saved?
Christ and the religions: restrictivism, wider hope, inclusivism and pluralism

Christians agree that Christ is Lord and saviour but disagree on what this means for the billions who have lived and died without hearing the gospel or who sincerely follow other faiths. The debate intensified with global encounter, Vatican II and the rise of religiously plural societies.

Scripture says faith comes by hearing and that there is no other name. All have sinned and are without excuse. If people could be saved without the gospel, the apostles’ urgency would make no sense. Our task is not to speculate about other ways but to go and tell.

Christ alone saves, but God’s mercy is wider than our knowledge. Abel, Job and Melchizedek were saved by faith without knowing Jesus’ name; God will judge each by the light they had. We may hope, while still telling everyone the good news in full.

The Word enlightens every person coming into the world. God’s grace can reach people through what is true and holy in their own traditions, always as the grace of Christ and oriented toward his Church. Dialogue honours that grace; mission brings it to fullness.

It is implausible that the God of love would confine salvation to one tradition that most humans never encountered. The great faiths produce saints and transform lives; they are different human responses to the one Real. Humility, not superiority, should mark our relations with them.
Justin speaks of seeds of the Word among the Greeks.
Cyprian: no salvation outside the Church.
Florence’s Cantate Domino gives the strict reading.
Holy Office rejects Feeney’s strict view.
Vatican II’s Nostra Aetate and Lumen Gentium 16.
Lausanne Covenant rejects universalism and syncretism.
Pinnock and Sanders argue for a wider hope.

Unresolved. The Catholic Church officially holds inclusivism within Christ’s unique mediation; Orthodox churches generally leave the fate of others to God’s mercy; evangelicals divide between restrictivism and wider hope; pluralism is found mainly in liberal Protestantism and academic theology.
Shapes motivation and methods of mission.
Debates within evangelicalism over inclusivism and universalism.
